Contrast Kings: 5 Muscle Cars That Look Awesome With White Vinyl Roofs and Decals
16 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
Back when vinyl tops were a popular feature, some customers went with white ones and matching decals which, paired with a contrasting paint color, made already great-looking muscle cars look even better.
Apart from insane performance, the golden age of muscle cars remains arguably the most exciting era in American automotive history because of the timeless styling and factory customization options that were offered back then.
Among those options were the white vinyl top and white decals which, paired with the right exterior color, dramatically improved the elegance of some models.
While white vinyl tops and decals were available on many performance models from that exciting era, the following five pulled off that elegant contrasting look better than anything else roaming the streets.
1968 Dodge Charger R/T Photo: Mecum Auctions The Charger started life in 1964 as a upscale coupe with a dramatic fastback roofline, one that was developed specifically to rival AMC’s popular Marlin .
While the model did succeed in outselling its rival, for the 1968 model year, Dodge completely redesigned the car and moved it from the affordable personal luxury coupe segment to muscle car territory.
The second-generation Charger was available in a tame yet affordable base specification, but the main attraction was the performance-oriented R/T (Road and Track) trim.
Photo: Mecum Auctions When this option was chosen, the Charger got a potent standard V8 or an optional one with even more oomph, such as the range-toping 426 HEMI .
The R/T came with a rear stripe package, which could be ordered in white. A vynil top was also available and optionally, it could be delivered in white instead of black.
With the white top and stripes, plus an eye-catching primary color such as Matador Red, the 1968 Dodge Charger R/T looked aggressive, yet also extremely elegant.
1968 Chevrolet Chevelle SS 396 Photo: Mecum Auctions Like most iconic muscle cars from the 1960s and 1970s, the Chevelle SS started out as a performance package, then morphed into a standalone performance model starting with the 1966 model year.
The Chevelle, including the SS performance model was available with a vinyl top for two-door hardtops from 1966. However, with the debut of the redesigned second-generation for 1968 model year, a white vinyl top option was added.
As you can see in these images, the white top, paired with the SS-exclusive white stripes and a contrasting primary color worked wonders on the already-gorgeous Chevelle SS, adding elegance to its naturally aggressive styling.
Photo: Mecum Auctions Like its immediate predecessors, the 1968 Chevelle SS came with a standard 396-ci (6.5-liter) big-block V8 rated at 325 hp (RPO L35). But if that wasn’t enough, customers could choose one of the two optional high-output 396s rated at either 350 hp ((RPO L34) or 375 hp (RPO L78).
Regardless of the engine it was equipped with, the 1968 Chevrolet Chevelle SS 396 was an iconic muscle car that thrilled with its straight-line performance and its timeless styling.
While any exterior color, vinyl top and decal combination looked great, the white top and decals contrasted by a vibrant exterior finish made this legendary muscle car turn even more heads.
1969 Chevrolet Camaro SS Photo: Mecum Auctions Surprisingly, GM brands took several years to come up with an answer to Ford’s Mustang, which sold like hotcakes since its debut in April 1964.
About two and a half years after the ‘Stang’s memorable New York World Fair debut, Chevrolet finally unveiled its first pony car in the shape of the Camaro.
With gorgeous styling and a wide range of options, including serious performance trims, the original Camaro went toe-to-toe with the Mustang and, although it never outsold its rival, it still became one of Chevrolet’s most revered models.
Photo: Mecum Auctions The first-gen Camaro entered its last year on the market in 1969 and it was offered with more options than ever before.
Among those options were, of course, white vinyl roofs for hardtop variants, including the high-performance SS, which could also be ordered with matching white hockey stripes.
As standard, the 1969 Camaro SS was powered by a 350-ci (5.7-liter) small-block rated at 300 hp, but customers could choose an optional 396, which was available in three distinct output variants, ranging from 325 to 375 hp.
However, when equipped with a white vinyl top , white stripes and a contrasting color, the 1969 Camaro SS looked incredibly good, regardless of the engine stuffed between its shock towers.
1970 Plymouth GTX Photo: Mecum Auctions For the 1967 model year, Plymouth introduced a new sub-model called GTX to the Belvedere range.
Available as a two-door hardtop or convertible, the GTX offered premium options and potent engines, instantly becoming one of the most impressive gentleman’s muscle cars.
While the Road Runner , it’s cheaper, no-frills performance sibling became way more popular following its debut for the 1968 model year, the GTX continued to be available as a premium, upscale muscle car.
Photo: Mecum Auctions For the epic 1970 model year, the GTX received a thorough styling refresh that included redesigned front and rear ends, a new hood on selects engine options and a new strip package, which could be ordered in white or black.
A vinyl roof was available as an option, one which most customers went for. However, a few customers went for the white vinyl roof and matching decals, combined with a primary color from the High Impact palette, which resulted in one of the most beautiful muscle cars that money could buy.
As you can see in the images above, a 1970 GTX finished in the High Impact color called “In Violet Metallic” looked absolutely amazing when combined with a white top and matching stripes, regardless if it was powered by the standard 440 cu in (7.2-liter) Super Commando rated at 375 hp, the optional 390-hp 440 Six-Barrel, or the range-topping, 425-hp 426 HEMI.
1970 Oldsmobile 4-4-2 Photo: Mecum Auctions While Pontiac is widely credited with kickstarting the muscle car craze in 1964 when it introduced the GTO, GM siblings Oldsmobile was the first brand to come up with an answer in the shape of the Cutlass-based 4-4-2.
The original 1964 4-4-2 wasn’t as epic as the GTO, but thanks to Oldsmobile’s tireless effort to improve it, the muscle car became a legend in the years that followed .
Perhaps the most impressive iteration of the 4-4-2 was offered during the memorable 1970 model year when it received a potent, 365-hp 455-ci (7.5-liter) Rocket V8 which could be made even more powerful with the addition of the W-30 performance package.
Photo: Mecum Auctions With or without the W-30 option, the 1970 4-4-2 was one of the most epic performance rides of the year and one of the greatest gentleman’s muscle cars ever created.
The epic model looked extremely well in any available color and decal combination. However, when equipped with a white vinyl top, matching side and hood stripes and a vibrant primary color, it looked even better.
